title: The Washer: a Disc With a Bite Out of It

steps.body:
Revolve the region **between two curves** and each strip sweeps out not a disc but a **washer** — a coin with a hole punched through it.

Outer radius R = the top curve. Inner radius r = the bottom one. The face is the big circle minus the small one:

**π(R² − r²)**

And once again: slice, measure the slice, add them up. Only the measurement changed.

widget.prompt: Revolve the region between y = x (outer) and y = x² (inner) on [0, 1]. Inspect a slice — it is a washer — then raise the count until the sum reaches within 0.005 of the exact 2π/15 ≈ 0.4189.
widget.successFeedback: Each slice is π(R² − r²) — the big face minus the hole. And look at the ends: at x = 0 and x = 1 the two curves MEET, so R = r and the washer has no metal in it at all. The solid pinches to nothing at both ends, exactly where the region did.
widget.lowFeedback: The sum is under 2π/15. The left and right rules both undershoot a region that pinches at both ends — raise the count, or try the midpoint rule.
widget.highFeedback: The sum is over 2π/15. The midpoint rule overshoots here — raise the count and it will settle down.

predict.prompt: What changes when the number of volume slices increases?

options.label: Slices become thinner and the estimate usually improves
The cross-section formula is no longer needed

predict.reveal: Refinement reduces slice thickness while preserving the same cross-section rule, bringing the sum closer to the limiting volume.

cml.actionGoal: Refine cross-sectional slices and connect their accumulated volume estimate to a limiting integral.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the controlling quantity in this sliceSum away from the successful state. Which invariant remains true, and which visible consequence changes?

explanation.prompt: Why does a slice sum become a volume integral?

options.label: Each cross-sectional area is multiplied by thickness, and refinement takes the sum to a limit.
options.feedback: Exactly—this identifies the governing mechanism rather than only the final pattern.

options.label: Only the base area is needed.
options.feedback: That describes an appearance or shortcut, not the invariant that makes the relationship hold.

options.label: The number of slices itself is the volume.
options.feedback: The live model contradicts that claim when its control is changed.

steps.body: Subtract the AREAS, not the radii.
explanationVariants: The face is πR² − πr² = π(R² − r²). It is NOT π(R − r)² — subtracting the radii first and then squaring is a different number entirely.
With R = 3 and r = 1: the true face is π(9 − 1) = 8π, while π(3 − 1)² = 4π. Half the answer.

widget.prompt: A washer has outer radius 3 and inner radius 1. What is its face area?

options.label: π(3² − 1²) = 8π
options.feedback: Right — subtract the AREAS. The big circle is 9π, the hole is π, and what is left is 8π.

options.label: π(3 − 1)² = 4π
options.feedback: That subtracts the RADII and then squares, which is a different number — half the truth. Square first, subtract second.

options.label: π(3² + 1²) = 10π
options.feedback: The hole is REMOVED, not added. The face is 9π − π = 8π.

options.label: π(3)² = 9π
options.feedback: That is the face with no hole at all. The inner circle of area π has been punched out.

explanationVariants: Outer radius x gives x²; inner radius x² gives x⁴. The difference is integrated, not the radii.

widget.prompt: Revolve the region between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1] about the x-axis. Find the volume, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is π/5 — the volume of the INNER solid alone (y = x² revolved). You must subtract it FROM the outer one: π(1/3 − 1/5).
That is π/3 — the OUTER solid alone (y = x revolved). The hole has not been punched out yet.
That is half the answer. π(1/3 − 1/5) = π(2/15) ≈ 0.419.

steps.body:
So the whole course is one sentence, repeated:

**Slice the region. Measure ONE slice. Add them up.**

An area measures a slice's **height**. A disc measures **πr²**. A washer measures **π(R² − r²)**. The slicing never changes; the summing never changes. Only the measurement does — and that is the only thing you ever have to work out.

explanationVariants: Height for an area; πr² for a disc; π(R² − r²) for a washer. Same slicing, same summing, three measurements.
If you can say what one slice is worth, you have already written the integral.

widget.prompt: Match each quantity to what you measure on ONE slice.

right.label: πr², with r the height of the curve

pairErrors.feedback: A plain disc has no hole — its face is πr². The subtraction only appears when the region has a gap under it.
A washer is a VOLUME, so its slice is measured in square units of face, not in height.

widget.missFeedback: Ask what ONE slice is worth. That measurement is the integrand, and the rest is bookkeeping.
widget.successFeedback: Slice, measure, sum. The measurement is the only thing that ever changes — which is why this course is much shorter than it looks.

hints: Outer radius R = 2 (the horizontal line y = 2). Inner radius r = x.
The face is π(2² − x²) = π(4 − x²).
V = π∫₀² (4 − x²) dx = π[4x − x³/3]₀².
explanationVariants: Sanity check: the outer solid is a cylinder of radius 2 and length 2, volume 8π ≈ 25.13; the cone drilled out of it is 8π/3 ≈ 8.38; and 25.13 − 8.38 = 16.75 ✓.

widget.prompt: Revolve the region between y = 2 (outer) and y = x (inner) on [0, 2] about the x-axis. Find the volume, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 8π — the whole CYLINDER, with no cone drilled out of it. Subtract the inner solid: 8π − 8π/3 = 16π/3.
That is 8π/3 — the CONE that gets removed, not what is left behind.
That is 16/3 × 3, or a dropped π. The answer is 16π/3 ≈ 16.755.

widget.fallbackFeedback: V = π∫₀² (4 − x²) dx = π(8 − 8/3) = 16π/3 ≈ 16.755 — and indeed the cylinder (8π) minus the cone (8π/3) gives exactly that.

takeaways: A washer's face is π(R² − r²) — subtract the AREAS, never the radii.
R is the far curve from the axis and r is the near one, so the hole is what the gap under the region sweeps out.
Area, disc, washer: same slicing, same summing, three measurements. Work out what ONE slice is worth and the integral writes itself.
steps.teaser: Still to come in this course: known cross-sections, average value, and motion revisited as ∫|v|.

concept.body: Two circles, one inside the other. Work out the BIG face, work out the HOLE, and subtract: π R² − π r². Squaring comes first and subtracting comes second — reversing them gives a different (and wrong) number.

explanationVariants: Squaring first is what makes the answer right: π(5 − 3)² would be only 4π.

widget.prompt: A washer has outer radius 5 and inner radius 3. Find its face area, to two decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is π(5 − 3)² = 4π — you subtracted the radii and then squared. Square FIRST: π(25 − 9) = 16π.
That is π(5²) = 25π — the outer circle with no hole punched out.
